title: A Very Bad 24 Hours for Crypto
excerpt: This is an edition of Over/Under, a newsletter on the latest in prediction markets, gambling, and the evolution of everyday risk
body: This is an edition of Over/Under, a newsletter on the latest in prediction markets, gambling, and the evolution of everyday risk
Last night, hackers stole approximately $6.3 billion from Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange
The whole thing reportedly took about 20 minutes

It was the biggest theft in the history of the sector, and also probably the biggest financial heist of all time, topping the $1.5 billion ByBit hack of 2025 and Sadam Hussein’s $1 billion robbery of the Central Bank of Iraq in 2003
Binance says that about half of the stolen funds have been “frozen”—meaning that they’re effectively banned from being used in future transactions
North Korean hackers are thought to have been responsible
In the hours before the attack, though, a smaller heist was roiling a different corner of digital finance: Yesterday afternoon, at least $2.6 million was reportedly drained from Polymarket accounts
Polymarket’s international platform, which until last month hosted the majority of the company’s trading volume, runs on blockchain technology
But the attacks had different origins, and there’s no evidence that the two are connected
Binance is saying that its hack may have involved a compromised laptop, as well as “additional points of breach”; thieves took money that was stored on the exchange
On Polymarket, hackers exploited a flaw in a third-party provider, allowing them to access users’ accounts
It was the firm’s second security lapse since June
Both platforms say they plan to cover the losses in full
But in crypto, getting your money back isn’t a guarantee
Despite the technical differences and massive disparity in scale, yesterday’s hacks are a reminder that crypto-backed platforms of all kinds can still come with fundamental risks

Unlike Kalshi, which has a single U.S. exchange for its domestic and international customers, Polymarket’s operations are split down the middle: Polymarket.com and Polymarket.us are two separate exchanges
When you make a bet on the U.S. site, your trade is settled in dollars
On the international site, everything is settled in crypto

Both traditional financial firms and blockchain-backed systems face immense cybersecurity challenges —and the crypto industry has done a lot of growing up since 2022—but with crypto, customers typically have less recourse when things go wrong
Although deposits at U.S. banks are technically IOUs, they tend to be really good IOUs
If you ask for your money, you can be pretty confident that it will be there
If the bank fails, you’re guaranteed to get some of it back, thanks to the miracle of FDIC insurance

Polymarket, like Binance, isn’t a bank, and its international platform isn’t overseen by the American regulatory system. (Both companies’ independent U.S. platforms, which are subject to onshore regulations, were entirely unaffected by these attacks.) Users may get their money back this time, as the firms have promised, but that’s not always the case—not all companies have the funds to repay their customers
They’re not necessarily obligated to, either
Polymarket’s ties to crypto go back to its founding, in 2020, a moment when the industry was seen as a kind of Wild West
Early on, users could make bets on the site only if they were willing to ditch old-school money for digital tokens

Polymarket didn’t even have a domestic, non-crypto platform until late last year—and until very recently , it was seeing less volume than the international site. (The demographics for crypto and prediction markets still have some overlap too.) This isn’t the end for Polymarket, and it’s certainly not the end for crypto, which has lately proved itself to be incredibly resilient. (Bitcoin is down a few thousand dollars since last night, but it hasn’t tanked nearly as much as you might expect after a disruption of this scale.) Still, the timing is unfortunate for the company
As I wrote on Wednesday, next week’s election coverage will put prediction markets in front of even more people

Users who have lost confidence in the company may end up switching over to Polymarket’s main competitor, Kalshi; users who aren’t familiar with prediction markets will have yet another reason to avoid them
Americans are already broadly skeptical of these firms’ push into politics
Polymarket’s link to crypto—and to the chaos of the past 24 hours—could further entrench that distrust
Possible Futures In every edition, I’ll share my thoughts on a few news stories I’m watching
On Wednesday, Utah’s attorney general filed 14 criminal charges against Kalshi and its co-founders, alleging that the company has been running a gambling platform against state rules

Both DraftKings and FanDuel have pulled some of their markets from the state, and Commodity Futures Trading Commission Chairman Michael Selig has pushed back, writing that Utah’s move sets a “dangerous precedent.” The agency is also suing the state (and many others ), alleging that prediction markets can be regulated only on the federal level.

title: The State Department Is in Disarray
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
Many a heavy-handed metaphor has been constructed on the claim that Washington, D.C., is built on a swamp
This hoary cliché is also, for the most part, untrue —but the neighborhood Foggy Bottom, home to the State Department, really is former marshland
Stories of decadence, deviousness, and ineptitude within the current Trump administration are a dime a dozen, even at current inflation rates

The Justice Department acts as a private law firm for the president; the Department of Health and Human Services seems dedicated to undermining both; the Hegseth Pentagon is breaking globes, both physically and metaphorically
Yet the State Department has escaped some of the taint that has attached to other departments and agencies
This may be because the exploits elsewhere are so blatant, and because Secretary of State Marco Rubio has a reputation as one of the more serious figures in the administration
Whatever the reasons, the State Department may deserve more opprobrium than it has received
One of the guiding philosophies of the second Trump presidency, imported from Project 2025, is that personnel is policy: The success of an administration depends on who staffs it
Perhaps holding Kimberly Guilfoyle , the ousted ambassador to Greece who was allegedly selling access, against the department would be unfair
After all, she was a political choice, likely selected as a thank-you from the president whose campaign she assisted, and to whose son she was previously engaged
But other appointments cannot be so easily explained away
One example is Darren Beattie, whose title is senior adviser for Western Hemisphere affairs
He has particular interest in policy toward Brazil, where the administration has worked to assist the right-wing movement associated with the Bolsonaro family; he is also president of the U.S
Institute of Peace, on which Trump has scrawled his own name
Beattie’s career shows the difference between the first and second Trump administrations: When his speech to white nationalists was revealed during the first, he was fired
In the second, he was welcomed back and given a plum role
One of his colleagues now is Nate Hochman

Once seen as a rising star of mainstream conservatism, Hochman went from National Review to the 2024 presidential campaign of Ron DeSantis, from which he was fired for sharing a video featuring Nazi imagery

After a pit stop working for Senator Eric Schmitt of Missouri, who has regularly made ethnonationalist comments (yes, he’s also the guy with the Jack Smith gaffe ), he landed at the State Department, where he is reportedly Rubio’s chief speechwriter
This might explain why the secretary’s recent speech in Athens was so obsessed with supposed threats to the West
The overlapping politics does not appear to be coincidental

Jeremy Carl, who has warned that “white culture” is imperiled, missed out on a chance to join Beattie and Hochman only when his Senate hearing in February completely derailed over offensive old tweets and his inability to explain his own views
The department now has an “ Office of Remigration ,” using a white-nationalist shibboleth for ethnic cleansing
Some of the State Department’s hires are questionable less for ideological than for personality reasons

Britt McHenry, a former ESPN personality who then deployed culture-war takes to become a mid-tier MAGA figure, joined the State Department last month as a press adviser, but her time there was short: She was resigned this past Friday after throwing a drink at a fan during a Washington Wizards game
Another recent departure is Paolo Zampolli, an old Trump hanger-on most famous for introducing the president and first lady

Zampolli snagged a State Department appointment as special envoy for global partnerships, focused on cultural affairs, but then quickly began meddling in issues that were not in his remit. (Not that he was aware what his remit was: “I didn’t even read the notification” to Congress about his role. “I don’t know about the notification,” he told Politico , saying he took direction from Trump.) Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau’s attempts to control Zampolli produced what Politico described as “a monthslong fight” conducted via “emails that at times included more than a dozen administration officials.” Shortly after that scoop, Zampolli was fired
Zampolli isn’t the only one inattentive to cultural diplomacy

Officials have been rampaging against a painting in the embassy in the Dominican Republic by the artist Kehinde Wiley, who is best known (perhaps not incidentally) for painting President Obama’s official portrait

Trump officials have referred to it as “very woke,” “aesthetically terrifying,” and a lesbian picnic . (The piece is much less titillating than this might suggest: It depicts four people posing over one of Wiley’s trademark floral patterns.) Are any top officials at the State Department above this chaos? Yes, but maybe not for long

My colleague Vivian Salama reported earlier this year on the deserted halls of the department, and The Washington Sun last week reported that leaders are working to promote political loyalists but squeeze out senior foreign-service officers, the most experienced members of the nonpolitical career staff trained in foreign relations. “The State Department is trying to get people to quit,” one officer told the Sun
Sometime soon, we might get a chance to learn what happens when diplomacy is fully in the hands of the least diplomatic people imaginable
Related: The end of diplomacy Marco Rubio’s disappearing Signal chat Here are three new stories from The Atlantic : Redistricting isn’t going as Republicans planned

The real threat of election interference A cynical ploy to block California’s wealth tax Today’s News An ICE officer was charged with aggravated assault with a deadly weapon after allegedly intentionally striking a Mexican construction worker with an SUV in Houston earlier this month
The worker, who was running away from officers, suffered a broken leg
ICE has denied that the collision was intentional, but local prosecutors say that surveillance footage contradicts the agency’s account

Binance, the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange, suspended deposits and withdrawals after hackers stole an estimated $6.3 billion in digital assets , in what could be the largest crypto heist in history
The company said it would cover customers’ losses and had frozen about $3 billion in stolen assets
A crypto research firm attributed the attack to North Korean hackers

title: When a Movie Hinges on a Kid’s Performance
excerpt: The film Josephine opens with one of the most upsetting sequences in any movie this year
body: The film Josephine opens with one of the most upsetting sequences in any movie this year
In it, the titular 8-year-old girl accidentally witnesses a woman being raped at a park near her home

In subsequent scenes, the filmmaker Beth de Araújo, who based the incident on an episode she experienced in childhood, carefully explores how the event affects Josephine and her family, and sheds light on larger questions: how parents can struggle to make sense of a child’s trauma, and how attempts to protect young people can yield more pain
Josephine is anchored by Mason Reeves, the actor who plays Josephine, who was 8 at the time of filming
Her performance sensitively conveys her character’s mixture of confusion, frustration, fear, and curiosity
Reeves is now 10, and she’s been enthusiastic, de Araújo told me, about acting in another project soon

De Araújo would rather she didn’t. “I hope and I believe Mason had a great experience on this,” she told me in September, “and I hope she also puts it aside for a while.” De Araújo is not the only director both working with children on films that have challenging themes and aiming to keep those young stars out of the spotlight

Cristian Mungiu, the writer-director of Fjord , has a similar wish for the adolescent actors who, in his film, give remarkably grounded performances as the children of a devout couple accused of child abuse. “I’m trying to encourage them to think twice before they consider acting as something they want to do for their lives,” Mungiu told me
The filmmakers’ hesitation is understandable
Children who grow up on sets are vulnerable to being physically and emotionally exploited, as numerous documentaries and memoirs have made clear
And the emotional toll of subsequent fame can lead to troubled adulthoods, as the recent deaths of former child stars including Hayden Panettiere and RJ Mitte have helped demonstrate
But these concerns may be of particular importance when it comes to children appearing in movies with dark subject matter, such as Josephine and Fjord
Zuri Pryor-Graves, an intimacy coordinator and a former therapist for child actors, told me that young performers immersed in intense environments often fail to notice when they’re overworked

Tight production timelines and the scrutiny of an adult crew isolate them from normal childhood experiences, including coming of age as themselves, rather than as their characters. “They’re in development stages where they’re learning who they are,” Pryor-Graves said. “Being able to create that separation is not something that’s built into a production schedule.” [ Read: The uncomfortable truth about child abuse in Hollywood ] In an op-ed for The New York Times in August, the former child actor Alison Pill echoed that concern: “At a time when kids are supposed to be forging our own identities, child actors have ours chosen for us by agents, casting directors and the public.” Pill called to end such work altogether. “The greatest storytellers should find a way to capture the world we live in without child actors,” she wrote, “for all our sakes.” Yet that idea seems impossible
Thoroughly adult stories that hinge on young performances are nothing new, and this year has seen a spate of such projects
Apart from de Araújo and Mungiu’s films, the drama Gentle Monster depicts a man who gets arrested for distributing child pornography; his 9-year-old son’s perspective becomes pivotal

This fall also brings the return of the Hunger Games franchise, and with it another round of youngsters fighting to the death, as well as the debut of Club Kid , a drama about a hard-partyer who discovers he has a 10-year-old son
And Primetime , a film dissecting the rise and fall of the reality-television series To Catch a Predator , features cameos from former child stars including Alex Winter and Jonathan Lipnicki
Their portrayals of some of the alleged pedophiles the TV show targeted flip the script, underlining how unprotected they themselves were as children
The directors I spoke with about this topic all agreed that young performers need extra care and attention
But the trouble with working with children is that no single method exists to ensure their healthy adulthoods

The question facing Hollywood, then, is whether the industry can ever truly place their youngest actors’ needs first—perhaps to the point of scrapping a film no matter the budgets, schedules, and egos involved

Projects involving child actors should move forward, de Araújo said, only if directors are genuinely confident those actors are capable of handling the pressure of being on a set. “If you don’t find them, you don’t find them,” she said. “You have to go back to the drawing board and start from scratch.” Let’s say you’re a child actor
In most cases, you’re accompanied by a supervisor on set who coordinates your schedule so you don’t exceed your legal work hours
You’re shuffled from hair and makeup to wardrobe, to rehearsal, to set

You’re surrounded by adults, whose attention you find intimidating or perhaps special; either way, you don’t want to be the problem. “Kids in front of the camera have a higher propensity for creating a bit of a false self,” Fran Walfish, a child psychologist based in Los Angeles, told me, “because they want to please everybody.” Marie Kreutzer, the writer-director of Gentle Monster , aimed to avoid this scenario
When she was casting for Johnny, the boy whose relationship with his father gets scrutinized, she made sure to “audition” the parents of her finalists
She talked with the caregivers at length about their reasons for allowing their kids to be on camera in a mature drama

Their level of enthusiasm for getting their children cast, she told me, could be telling. “When you have difficult conversations like that in the beginning, you immediately get a very good feeling about them and how they are as parents,” she explained
After the then-7-year-old Malo Blanchet was cast as Johnny, his parents asked whether he wanted them around while he filmed
Kreutzer said Blanchet declined because having them there seemed stressful

On set, Kreutzer tried to keep Blanchet from becoming overly attached to crew members. “Being the center of attention of a whole film crew for a while can really do something to you as a person when you are young,” Kreutzer said

She pointed out that the separation anxiety that comes at the end of filming can be disorienting, no matter a person’s age. “ We even get that wrong, you know?” she said. “When I’m shooting a film and I wrap, I always miss the people.” [ Read: How Daniel Radcliffe outran Harry Potter ] Every filmmaker I spoke with discussed the importance of creating distance between young actors’ normal life and the grown-up stories they help tell

Mungiu, of Fjord , calls his younger cast members “interpreters” rather than “actors,” and said he aims to give them simple, direct instructions about how to portray their characters. “We shouldn’t project our personalities as adults on children,” he said

Kreutzer said she wanted to explain the story of Gentle Monster to Blanchet in terms he would understand by offering him, as she put it, “a part of the truth.” She spoke with Blanchet’s parents about what he’d be able to handle; together, they agreed to describe Gentle Monster to him as a film about a mom and a dad having a hard time separating, a concept he grasped because he had friends whose parents had divorced
Josephine , with its story rooted in a traumatic sexual-assault case, required similar discretion, especially because Reeves is in almost every scene

De Araújo told me she worked closely with Reeves’s parents to come up with a plan that would let Reeves avoid undergoing the same emotional turmoil as Josephine, while still understanding her character’s arc

She and Reeves mapped out Josephine’s emotions by revisiting Reeves’s own memories; if Reeves had to portray Josephine being angry, she’d recall the time her sister ruined a drawing she made, for example
De Araújo hoped that this would protect the 8-year-old from being too immersed in the particulars of her character’s story

In addition, Reeves saw only portions of the script, was not on set for the filming of the opening scene, and was told that the movie boils down to “Josephine sees something bad and it makes her scared, and then the film is about Josephine overcoming her fear and being stronger,” de Araújo said

title: The Internet Might Need to Be Rebuilt From Scratch
excerpt: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube AI hacking swarms are poking holes across the internet at such a rate that some cybersecurity professionals h
body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube AI hacking swarms are poking holes across the internet at such a rate that some cybersecurity professionals have dubbed this month “Black October.” The AI-cybersecurity professional Alex Stamos argues that it’s time to be proactive rather than reactive, and that might mean rewriting the code for the internet in newer programming languages that could make all of our online systems and personal information safer
He joins the Galaxy Brain host Charlie Warzel to explain why that’s not as big of a deal as it sounds, and how we can all protect ourselves in the meantime
The following is a transcript of the episode: Alex Stamos: What we have to do, as people who work in cybersecurity, is: We have to shorten the Dark Age
We need to make sure the Library of Alexandria doesn’t burn, right? We have to do everything possible to make this as short as possible
And from my perspective, the best way to do that is to be proactive, not reactive, here
And to be proactive we can’t just wait for these bad things to happen; we have to intentionally re-architect things
There’s this endless string of bracing news events
But there’s another crisis looming as well
The digital infrastructure that powers our entire on- and offline lives is, according to the people who protect it, more vulnerable than ever
The internet as we know it is a very fragile ecosystem
So much of it is built off of code that’s written by humans—that is, by nature, full of flaws or bugs
Some of our critical digital infrastructure, it’s built off of decades-old technology that’s running on ancient code languages
But it is also, like any massive human endeavor, imperfect and full of vulnerabilities
One way to look at the history of cybersecurity is as a race between people who are looking to exploit all those vulnerabilities and the people who can fortify our systems and keep them secure
But in recent months, AI has threatened to change the dynamics of that race
AI agents—which are cheap, relentless, and highly capable hacker armies—are proving excellent at finding vulnerabilities in code
Sometimes, oftentimes, in places that humans had never thought to look
And the result has been this series of high-profile cybersecurity incidents, each one adding to this feeling that we’ve entered a new era
The rate of disclosures of incidents has been so intense that in recent weeks, cybersecurity professionals are referring to this month as Black October

Last week, the public found out that AI agents found vulnerability in PHP, which is a coding language that affects 70 percent of the internet, that could allow hackers to gain access to almost any server
On top of PHP, there have been disclosures in major software products like Node.js, which is software that’s used across countless important webpages and services on the internet
This is stuff that powers everything from supply chains to health-care companies

And the fear is that what we are seeing here is not some kind of aberration, but the beginning of this new normal—this period of time where everything from our power grids to our personal data may be uniquely vulnerable
And so I wanted to understand exactly how unprecedented this Black October moment really is, and what it means for the state of the internet and the possibilities of catastrophic events in the future
Alex Stamos is the chief information security officer at the AI company Cognition, and the former chief security officer at Facebook
He is not only on the forefront of this current crisis, but he’s also somebody who understands how massive digital organizations respond to the demands of an increasingly insecure internet
I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain . [ Music ] Warzel: Alex Stamos, welcome to Galaxy Brain
Stamos: Hey, thanks for having me, Charlie
Warzel: So we’re in the middle of what feels right now like this explosion of either AI-powered hacks or cybersecurity disclosures
Right now, people in your industry, and colloquially on places like X are referring to it as Black October
Can you walk me through what has changed fundamentally in the last two weeks? Stamos: Yeah
So we’re just kind of—this has honestly been a slow burn
But what’s been really interesting in this month is that finally attackers are getting the benefit from AI; where they have the ability to use AI to automate what we call kill chains
So you know, this is a term we have stolen from the military—where, when the military says “kill chain,” they mean to actually kill something
In the cyber world, those are the steps you take to break into a network and to do something
And traditionally, you could automate some parts of a kill chain

And just in the last several months, we’ve gotten to the point of where AI models—and especially the open-weight models, the models that you can run locally on hardware you run yourself, and even commodity hardware like these new Mac Studios that you can buy—are good enough that basically every step of the kill chain can be completely automated with AI
And so that has really changed the game here—where you can get rid of any human bottleneck
And that has completely changed the economics and the speed at which attackers can move
Warzel: So I’ve heard of this being talked about as a “disclosure wave,” meaning that it’s a disclosure of potential vulnerabilities and not a wave of attacks

title: The Currency of the Journal Article Is Collapsing
excerpt: Weak scholarship was once easy to spot at a glance: The signs included bad writing, a lack of relevant citations, and little engagement with previous scholarshi
body: Weak scholarship was once easy to spot at a glance: The signs included bad writing, a lack of relevant citations, and little engagement with previous scholarship, such as a paper that promised a “novel” conceptual framework without acknowledging the many other papers making similar claims
As an associate editor of a bioethics journal, I’d make a quick “desk reject” decision and not send these articles for peer review, which effectively killed any hope of publication
Now I can say: AI is affecting every part of academic publishing
Readers have started to notice that AI-assisted articles are slipping into journals
But AI is creating problems behind the scenes as well
Weak articles now arrive on my desk with fluent prose, plausible-sounding arguments, neatly organized sections, and citations that pass initial AI checks
Only with a deeper look does the AI use become apparent

There are sentences that have all of the trappings of real arguments, but that rarely make sense—like, say, “Algorithmic triage functions less as a clinical tool than as an infrastructure of deferred accountability.” There are citations that refer only to open-access or highly cited articles , because the most popular LLMs can’t readily access paywalled journal articles, so they rely on what’s either free or described at length elsewhere
Unfortunately, the scholars submitting papers aren’t the only ones using AI
One recent peer review that my journal received—from a senior scholar—read like an unedited cut-and-paste job from an LLM

The giveaway was that it criticized the authors for failing to cite a particular text—in this case, the fifth edition of the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders —when the paper did indeed cite it. [ Read: The rise of parasite authors ] Some of my own papers have received similarly suspicious peer reviews

A recent one of a paper that I had co-authored came in the telltale header-bullet style of ChatGPT, requesting 22 major and 14 minor edits on matters spanning ethics, statistics, experimental design, and machine learning
A review by a human typically comes from somewhere; I can usually tell, without knowing the name, whether a reviewer is a philosopher or a social scientist
But this review came from both everywhere and nowhere

The prose sparkled (human reviewers don’t take the time to polish text that no one but the authors and editors will see); the review quibbled with an inessential word and offered three synonyms to use instead (reviewers will object to a word or phrase, but they don’t usually supply a thesaurus-like menu of alternatives); and it questioned the year a reference was published (reviewers regularly check sources, but not the accuracy of small bibliographic details)
But as every academic knows, peer review has always been a highly imperfect process
One might imagine experts with deep knowledge of a paper’s topic or methods carefully reviewing each manuscript prior to publication

The reality is that those with relevant expertise are overwhelmed with review requests and almost never have the time to write one, particularly if the request comes from a lesser-known journal. (I learned this in my first years as a journal editor, when my review requests to top scholars were mostly ignored or declined.) Although many reviews are thoughtful, others come from people with tangential expertise. (Entire corners of the internet are dedicated to memes from “Reviewer 2,” a caricature of a pedantic scholar who has clearly misunderstood the paper.) When retractions or fabrications make the news , such as the 2024 Frontiers in Cell and Developmental Biology article that included an AI-generated image of a rat with oversize genitals, the public often reacts with outrage at the failure of the peer-review process
But as a journal editor, I’m surprised it doesn’t happen more often
AI has pushed this already flawed system of peer review to its breaking point
Journals are being inundated with manuscript submissions
Some journals have reported their submissions doubling or even tripling since ChatGPT was released, a few years ago
Across the Elsevier portfolio of journals, submissions were about twice as high in 2025 than in 2024
One journal reported having to double its editors—all unpaid volunteers—to handle the boom in submissions
Reviewing a growing number of submissions with a critical eye now takes time that minimally compensated or unpaid journal editors, including me, do not have

As a result, even as journal editors desk-reject more manuscripts, they are also sending more and more AI-assisted papers out for review, which in turn off-loads the work of picking apart AI-assisted articles to two or three other overworked scholars
These scholars are, in turn, receiving more and more review requests

In some cases, the cycle has become absurd: AI-assisted papers land with overworked editors, who send them to rushed reviewers, who in some cases use AI to write the review, which the authors revise and resubmit using AI
A recent study of 7.3 million journal articles published from 2020 to 2025 found that by 2025, more than half showed evidence of LLM assistance, up from 12 percent in 2023
These problems are most likely to afflict the humanities and social sciences, because conceptual argumentation is easier to mimic than experimental results
But AI can generate much of an article even in the hard sciences. [ Steven Strogatz: A mathematician reads the AI future ] The journal article has long been the currency of academic social capital
Most early-career academics can tell you offhand how many they have published, like a salesperson rattling off their most recent quarter’s numbers
This currency has remained valuable because, until recently, a good article was difficult to produce
Such scholarship required time, sometimes funding, and the expertise to design a study or work through an argument
Currencies collapse when people can no longer trust them

Even if a handful of top-tier journals can preserve the value of their articles, they cannot survive in an academic economy in which tens of thousands of other outlets cannot distinguish serious scholarship from work that just looks like it
Each week, I meet with my trainees to read and critique a journal article in our field
I recently assigned an article with a promising title that had been published in an established journal weeks earlier, which had looked fine after a skimmed read
But as we dissected it, we began to see all of the hallmarks of AI: the sheen without the substance, the citations that were slightly off, the odd absence of conceptual coherence
I’d been on a conference panel with one of the authors earlier that year

title: Israel’s Latest Last Chance to Save Itself
excerpt: I live on the same street in north Tel Aviv as Gali Baharav-Miara, Israel’s attorney general
body: I live on the same street in north Tel Aviv as Gali Baharav-Miara, Israel’s attorney general
Occasionally I see her walking through the neighborhood, a bodyguard following 20 feet behind
To the government and its supporters, she is an unelected official obstructing the elected right’s ability to govern
To liberal Israelis, she is one of the last institutional barriers between democracy and unchecked political power
The national argument plays itself out beneath my window
On Saturday nights, right-wing protesters gather outside her home, shouting, honking their horns, and demanding her dismissal
I’ve seen Mordechai David here, a right-wing activist who has become notorious for confronting prominent government opponents while filming them on his phone
On Friday afternoons, Baharav-Miara’s supporters take their place, wearing Gali, Guardian of Israel T-shirts and holding signs urging her to stay strong
The cafés open in the morning and we drink our coffee
Israelis have been predicting the end of Israel for as long as I can remember
In my liberal, secular circles, almost every election has been described as the decisive one, the last opportunity to save the country
If Menachem Begin wins, Israel is finished
If Benjamin Netanyahu returns—again—Israel is finished
Friends announce that this time they really will leave
Yet when the results arrive, and despair descends, the following morning most wake up, drink their coffee, and go to work

After voting on Tuesday, that’s what millions did on Wednesday. [ Graeme Wood: Israeli election results hazy, try again ] All of this is partly because Israelis are dramatic people, and Jewish history has given us good reason to be alert to impending disaster
It is also because leaving is harder than declaring an intention to leave
People have parents, children, jobs, homes, friends, and a language in which they know how to quarrel and make jokes
Besides, even extreme political change doesn’t immediately alter the texture of everyday life
As another election fades into history, school drop-off remains the same, as does the taste of that first cup of coffee

After the Yom Kippur War of 1973—the first war in which Israel seemed vulnerable and its victory uncertain—a wave of Israelis emigrated, shaken by the discovery that the Jewish state could not guarantee their safety
Ever since, departure has been both a real phenomenon and a national threat, uttered whenever the country disappoints us
We are forever leaving, and forever still here
The liberal panic about Begin in 1977 was not invented
He came from a political tradition that the Labor establishment had treated as dangerous and illegitimate, and his victory ended three decades of rule by the elites who had founded the state

Many secular Ashkenazi Israelis felt as if their country had been seized by strangers: nationalists, religious Jews, and Mizrahi voters whose families had come from Morocco, Iraq, and elsewhere in the Arab world

For decades, the Labor establishment had treated these immigrants as cultural inferiors, housing them first in impoverished transit camps and later in remote development towns, far from the country’s centers of power
Begin treated them not as backward newcomers requiring instruction, but as fellow Jews entitled to dignity and influence
Along the way, Begin changed Israel profoundly, not always for the better
He accelerated the West Bank settlements and helped push inflation into triple digits
Even worse, he led Israel into the disastrous 1982 Lebanon War, which drove the Palestine Liberation Organization from Beirut but left Israel trapped in a bloody and protracted occupation
Yet Begin also respected the democratic transfer of power that brought him to office
He also did not attempt to neutralize every institution capable of restraining him
Most important, in 1979 this lifelong nationalist signed a peace treaty with Egypt, agreeing to return the entire Sinai Peninsula; the withdrawal was completed three years later
In short, Begin recognized that holding power did not mean that every ideological dream had to be realized, or that compromise was treason
As Begin is often quoted as saying, the difficulties of peace are better than the agonies of war
Two decades after Begin, Sharon frightened the Israeli left for even more concrete reasons
He was a leading architect of the settlement project, and a ruthless army officer as far back as the 1950s

As Begin’s defense minister, Sharon was also found indirectly responsible for failing to prevent the Sabra and Shatila massacre, when a Lebanese Christian militia supported by Israel killed at least 1,300 people in Beirut
When Sharon was elected prime minister in 2001, many liberals again spoke as if the state had reached its final chapter

title: Eating disorders are on the rise. GLP-1s could make things worse.
excerpt: Eating disorders are surging globally: A new study in JAMA Psychiatry found anorexia and bulimia rose 71% between 1990 and 2023, affecting an estimated 18.1 mil
body: Eating disorders are surging globally: A new study in JAMA Psychiatry found anorexia and bulimia rose 71% between 1990 and 2023, affecting an estimated 18.1 million people—and experts say the true number affected by eating disorders is likely three times higher

Social media is fueling the crisis: TikTok's algorithm served users with eating disorders 4,343% more harmful content than those without—and clinicians say "thinspiration" trends can trigger new cases

GLP-1 drugs are making things worse: Experts are already seeing patients—some as young as 11—misusing weight-loss drugs " data-chronoton-post-id="1147838" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade
But to some clinical psychologists, they can represent something more sinister—a potential trigger for eating disorders
A new report suggests that the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa shot up between 1990 and 2023—by a whopping 71%
By 2023, there were an estimated 18.1 million people living with one of these two disorders
What’s worse is that the number is likely to be much higher than that once we factor in other eating disorders
And, disturbingly, those in the field are already starting to see GLP-1 weight-loss drugs exacerbating the issue
Cheri Levinson is a clinical psychologist at the University of Louisville in Kentucky who has specialized in eating disorders for almost 20 years
She says she’s now seeing more patients with more severe symptoms than at any other time in her career, and that many of them are misusing GLP-1s. “This is the worst I’ve seen things,” she says
Eating disorders are mental health conditions in which people’s eating behaviors impact their health
They include anorexia nervosa (defined by a fear of weight gain), bulimia nervosa (in which people binge and purge), binge eating disorder, and others
It’s thought that some people have a genetic predisposition to certain eating disorders, but that some external factor is what triggers their onset
That might be stress, or social pressure to be skinny
Often, simply restricting food intake can trigger an eating disorder, says Levinson
Eating disorders—along with the pressure to look thin—were already prevalent in the 1990s (the  heroin chic era springs to mind)

To find out how things might have changed since then, Ruhai Bai at the Children’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University in China and his colleagues pulled together data from studies and surveys conducted on populations around the world
The team used statistical models to fill in any data gaps
That research allowed the researchers to estimate the annual incidence of two eating disorders—anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa—for each of 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023
They also estimated the impact those disorders had on global health by calculating their disability-adjusted life years (one  DALY represents a year of healthy life lost)
The findings, published in JAMA Psychiatry on Wednesday, are unsettling
Between 1990 and 2023, there was a 71% increase in the incidence of those two eating disorders, the team found
Those conditions had a huge impact on global health, too
In 2023, they “cost the world the equivalent of about 3.83 million years of healthy life,” says Bai
Bai and his colleagues expect these figures to continue to rise
In 2023, an estimated 18.1 million people had either anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa; by 2050, the team predict, the two conditions could affect 21.8 million people
Those two conditions represent less than half of all eating disorders, says Levinson, who was not involved in Bai’s study
The true impact of these disorders is “probably three times the rate that they’re reporting,” she says
Bai and his colleagues didn’t explore the reasons for this rise (although Bai points out that it can’t be entirely explained by population growth)

So how did we get here? Social media may have played a role. “Social media comparisons, influencers, challenges, diet trends can all be precipitating … events for an eating disorder,” says Cynthia Bulik, a clinical psychologist at the University of North Carolina, who was not involved in the new study
Bulik has been studying and treating eating disorders since the early 1980s. “Between 1990 and 2023 there has clearly been an upsurge of those types of environmental exposures,” she says

Many social media users are exposed to filtered and modified images of skinny influencers who may have undergone cosmetic surgery or extreme dieting and who are promoting “thinspiration” or “fitspiration” content
But users with eating disorders appear to be more likely to engage with this content—and to be fed more of it as a result

When researchers at the University of Melbourne  investigated this phenomenon a couple of years ago, they found that the algorithms of TikTok users with eating disorders delivered 4343% more “toxic eating disorder videos” than those of users who didn’t have the disorders
They also got more content focused on dieting or exercising
Many were fed over 1000 problematic videos per month
Bulik describes social media as “quicksand” for people with, or at risk of, eating disorders
The covid-19 pandemic—and the social isolation that accompanied lockdowns—also appears to have contributed to the rise in eating disorders
Research conducted in 2021 found that the number of people hospitalized with eating disorders in the US doubled between 2018 and 2020
Researchers don’t yet have good data on how trends in eating disorders might have progressed since 2023
quotes: trends can trigger new cases GLP-1 drugs are making things worse: Experts are already seeing patients—some as young as 11—misusing weight-loss drugs

title: Zombies are real – just ask the parasites taking over the bodies and brains of insects and rodents, leading them to their doom
url:
<title>Zombies are real – just ask the parasites taking over the bodies and brains of insects and rodents, leading them to their doom</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766774/original/file-20261016-50-crkhu4.jpeg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C136%2C2048%2C1365&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The fungus _Ophiocordyceps_ (stalk growing out of the ant&#39;s head) helped inspire the video game and show &quot;The Last of Us.&quot;</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.inaturalist.org/photos/407452035">Denis Zabin/iNaturalist</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Zombies have taken many forms in popular culture. In Michael Jackson’s “<a href="https://youtu.be/sOnqjkJTMaA">Thriller</a>” music video, corpses climb out of their graves and perform an impressively coordinated dance. In HBO’s “<a href="https://theconversation.com/pancakes-wont-turn-you-into-a-zombie-as-in-hbos-the-last-of-us-but-fungi-in-flour-have-been-making-people-sick-for-a-long-time-200428">The Last of Us</a>,” a fungus infects humans, takes over their bodies and turns them into hosts that help spread the infection. Even Plankton has tried his hand at taking control of another organism in “<a href="https://spongebob.fandom.com/wiki/Plankton!">SpongeBob SquarePants</a>.”</p>

<p>These examples are fictional, but they all play with the same unsettling idea: Can one organism take control of another, even after they’re dead? In nature, the answer is not quite as dramatic, but some parasites and fungi come surprisingly close. </p>

<p>I spend much of my time as a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=Xe78w-wAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">biomedical engineer and synthetic biologist</a> thinking about how biological systems sense signals, process information and change their behavior. That is part of what makes the idea of one organism taking control of another so fascinating to me.</p>

<p>Some parasites and fungi can <a href="https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev.ento.54.110807.090556">alter the behavior of a living host</a> in ways that benefit the parasite. They do not bring the dead back to life. Instead, they interfere with biological systems that control movement, motivation and decision-making. </p>

<h2>Zombie ants and fungi</h2>

<p>The best-known example of a parasite changing its host’s behavior is the <a href="https://www.loc.gov/everyday-mysteries/categories/biology-and-human-anatomy/item/whats-up-with-zombie-ants/">“zombie ant” fungus</a>, <em>Ophiocordyceps</em>, which helped inspire “The Last of Us.”</p>

<p>The life cycle of the zombie ant fungus begins when fungal spores land on an ant. The spores stick to the ant’s outer surface and eventually break through it, allowing the fungus to enter the body. Once inside, the fungus grows and spreads while the ant is still alive. The infection can develop over several weeks before the most <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s00253-024-13332-x">dramatic changes in the ant’s behavior</a> begin. </p>

<p>Eventually, the infected ant leaves the colony and begins wandering and climbing vegetation. This behavior moves the ant away from its normal habitat and into a location that favors fungal reproduction and dispersal. Near the end of the infection, the ant bites tightly onto a leaf, twig or other plant surface and remains attached in what researchers call a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s00253-024-13332-x">death grip</a>. After the ant dies, the fungus consumes the remaining tissues and produces a stalk from the ant’s body. This structure releases spores that can fall on other ants below and begin the cycle again. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766757/original/file-20261016-60-cfyshl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Dead ant biting the under" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766757/original/file-20261016-60-cfyshl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766757/original/file-20261016-60-cfyshl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=864&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766757/original/file-20261016-60-cfyshl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=864&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766757/original/file-20261016-60-cfyshl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=864&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766757/original/file-20261016-60-cfyshl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1086&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766757/original/file-20261016-60-cfyshl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1086&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766757/original/file-20261016-60-cfyshl.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1086&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">These ants show the characteristic death grip and head stalk of an <em>Ophiocordyceps</em> infection.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0004835">Pontoppidan et al/PLoS One</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>How does the fungus make the ant do this? You might imagine fungal cells invading the ant’s brain and taking control. Surprisingly, researchers examining infected ants before death found extensive fungal growth <a href="https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.200683">throughout the body and around muscle fibers</a>, but not inside the brain. Fungal cells can form networks around the ant’s muscles, suggesting that the ability to manipulate behavior may involve communication between the fungus and multiple host tissues rather than direct control of the brain.</p>

<p>The death grip provides an especially striking example of how the fungus can manipulate its host’s muscles. The jaw muscles of infected ants are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.200683">heavily colonized by the fungus</a>, showing signs of extreme contraction. There are also signs that the fungus may be releasing molecules near these tissues. Yet motor neurons and connections between nerves and muscles can remain intact. Together, these findings suggest that the fungus may alter the machinery controlling muscle contraction rather than simply destroying it. </p>

<p>Scientists still do not know exactly what causes ants to undergo the entire sequence of wandering, climbing and biting. While researchers have <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s00253-024-13332-x">identified fungal genes</a> associated with proteins, toxins and other compounds that could affect chemical signaling in the host, many of these possible mechanisms have not yet been proved. </p>

<p>That uncertainty is part of what makes the system so fascinating. The fungus does not appear to flip a single “zombie switch.” Instead, it may change several biological systems at once until the ant behaves in a way that benefits the fungus. </p>

<h2>How to create a zombie</h2>

<p><em>Ophiocordyceps</em> is not the only organism capable of changing a host’s behavior. </p>

<p>The <a href="https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0010019">emerald jewel wasp, <em>Ampulex compressa</em></a>, uses a very different strategy: It injects venom into a cockroach’s nervous system. The cockroach is not paralyzed, but it becomes much less likely to start moving on its own or to escape. The wasp can then lead it to a burrow and lay an egg on it. </p>

<p>Researchers have shown that the venom reduces activity in parts of the nervous system involved in starting movement. In other words, the cockroach can still walk, but its drive to do so has been changed. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766767/original/file-20261016-50-cke954.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Wasp and cockroach head to head on a cement block" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766767/original/file-20261016-50-cke954.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766767/original/file-20261016-50-cke954.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766767/original/file-20261016-50-cke954.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766767/original/file-20261016-50-cke954.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=338&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766767/original/file-20261016-50-cke954.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766767/original/file-20261016-50-cke954.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766767/original/file-20261016-50-cke954.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=424&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">This cockroach takes its marching orders from the emerald jewel wasp.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Vespa_Joia_arrastando_barata.jpg">JMGM/Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><a href="https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/how-a-parasitic-worm-forces-praying-mantises-to-drown-themselves/">Hairworms take behavioral manipulation</a> one step further by leading their hosts toward their own demise. Some species infect praying mantises or crickets and grow inside them while the insect is still alive. When the worm is ready to reproduce, the infected host becomes unusually attracted to light, which may draw it toward the shiny surface of water. The host enters the water, where the worm escapes from its body and begins the next stage of its life cycle. For the host that cannot swim, that behavior can be fatal.</p>

<p>Researchers are still working out exactly how the parasite causes this change, but studies have found changes in proteins in the host’s brain as the parasite manipulates it. In effect, the parasite appears to hijack the host’s sensory and behavioral machinery to guide it somewhere it would not normally go.  </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/YB6O7jS_VBM?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Unfortunately for crickets, hairworms also find them good hosts.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Behavioral manipulation also occurs in mammals. <a href="https://theconversation.com/toxoplasma-is-a-common-parasite-that-causes-birth-defects-but-the-us-doesnt-screen-for-it-during-pregnancy-232936"><em>Toxoplasma gondii</em></a> can infect many warm-blooded animals, but it reproduces in cats. </p>

<p>While rodents normally avoid cat odors, those infected with the parasite can lose some of that natural aversion and even <a href="https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0608310104">become attracted to cat odors</a>. This change could increase the chance that an infected rodent is eaten by a cat, allowing the parasite to complete its life cycle.</p>

<h2>More than mind control</h2>

<p>These examples show why “mind control” is an imperfect description of how parasites manipulate their hosts. Parasites do not need to control every action that their host makes. They may only need to change one key behavior: whether to climb, whether to walk away, whether to enter water or whether to avoid a predator. </p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766772/original/file-20261016-60-nvxzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Microscopy image of an oblong blob with smaller circles within" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766772/original/file-20261016-60-nvxzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766772/original/file-20261016-60-nvxzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766772/original/file-20261016-60-nvxzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766772/original/file-20261016-60-nvxzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=600&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766772/original/file-20261016-60-nvxzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766772/original/file-20261016-60-nvxzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766772/original/file-20261016-60-nvxzy9.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=754&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption"><em>Toxoplasma gondii</em> cycle between rodents, cats and humans.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Toxoplasma_gondii_(2).jpg">AJ Cann/Wikimedia Commons</a>, <a class="license" href="http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/">CC BY-SA</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>There is no single “zombie switch.” Behavior emerges from communication between the nervous system, muscles and other tissues throughout the body. Different parasites have evolved different ways to interfere with those systems.</p>

<p>So biology cannot create the dancing dead of “Thriller” or the infected humans of “The Last of Us.” But if a zombie is a living organism whose normal behavior has been redirected by another organism, nature has already created plenty of them. </p>

<p>Studying these real-life zombies may help scientists understand not only how parasites manipulate their hosts, but also how normal behavior is generated and controlled in the first place.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292955/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: The fungus _Ophiocordyceps_ (stalk growing out of the ant's head) helped inspire the video game and show "The Last of Us." Denis Zabin/iNaturalist , CC BY-SA Zombies have taken many forms in popular culture
In Michael Jackson’s “ Thriller ” music video, corpses climb out of their graves and perform an impressively coordinated dance
In HBO’s “ The Last of Us ,” a fungus infects humans, takes over their bodies and turns them into hosts that help spread the infection

Even Plankton has tried his hand at taking control of another organism in “ SpongeBob SquarePants .” These examples are fictional, but they all play with the same unsettling idea: Can one organism take control of another, even after they’re dead? In nature, the answer is not quite as dramatic, but some parasites and fungi come surprisingly close
I spend much of my time as a biomedical engineer and synthetic biologist thinking about how biological systems sense signals, process information and change their behavior
That is part of what makes the idea of one organism taking control of another so fascinating to me
Some parasites and fungi can alter the behavior of a living host in ways that benefit the parasite
Instead, they interfere with biological systems that control movement, motivation and decision-making

Zombie ants and fungi The best-known example of a parasite changing its host’s behavior is the “zombie ant” fungus , Ophiocordyceps , which helped inspire “The Last of Us.” The life cycle of the zombie ant fungus begins when fungal spores land on an ant
The spores stick to the ant’s outer surface and eventually break through it, allowing the fungus to enter the body
Once inside, the fungus grows and spreads while the ant is still alive
The infection can develop over several weeks before the most dramatic changes in the ant’s behavior begin
Eventually, the infected ant leaves the colony and begins wandering and climbing vegetation
This behavior moves the ant away from its normal habitat and into a location that favors fungal reproduction and dispersal
Near the end of the infection, the ant bites tightly onto a leaf, twig or other plant surface and remains attached in what researchers call a death grip
After the ant dies, the fungus consumes the remaining tissues and produces a stalk from the ant’s body
This structure releases spores that can fall on other ants below and begin the cycle again
These ants show the characteristic death grip and head stalk of an Ophiocordyceps infection
Pontoppidan et al/PLoS One , CC BY-SA How does the fungus make the ant do this? You might imagine fungal cells invading the ant’s brain and taking control
Surprisingly, researchers examining infected ants before death found extensive fungal growth throughout the body and around muscle fibers , but not inside the brain

Fungal cells can form networks around the ant’s muscles, suggesting that the ability to manipulate behavior may involve communication between the fungus and multiple host tissues rather than direct control of the brain
The death grip provides an especially striking example of how the fungus can manipulate its host’s muscles
The jaw muscles of infected ants are heavily colonized by the fungus , showing signs of extreme contraction
There are also signs that the fungus may be releasing molecules near these tissues
Yet motor neurons and connections between nerves and muscles can remain intact
Together, these findings suggest that the fungus may alter the machinery controlling muscle contraction rather than simply destroying it
Scientists still do not know exactly what causes ants to undergo the entire sequence of wandering, climbing and biting

While researchers have identified fungal genes associated with proteins, toxins and other compounds that could affect chemical signaling in the host, many of these possible mechanisms have not yet been proved
That uncertainty is part of what makes the system so fascinating
The fungus does not appear to flip a single “zombie switch.” Instead, it may change several biological systems at once until the ant behaves in a way that benefits the fungus
How to create a zombie Ophiocordyceps is not the only organism capable of changing a host’s behavior
The emerald jewel wasp, Ampulex compressa , uses a very different strategy: It injects venom into a cockroach’s nervous system
The cockroach is not paralyzed, but it becomes much less likely to start moving on its own or to escape
The wasp can then lead it to a burrow and lay an egg on it
Researchers have shown that the venom reduces activity in parts of the nervous system involved in starting movement
In other words, the cockroach can still walk, but its drive to do so has been changed
This cockroach takes its marching orders from the emerald jewel wasp
JMGM/Wikimedia Commons , CC BY-SA Hairworms take behavioral manipulation one step further by leading their hosts toward their own demise
Some species infect praying mantises or crickets and grow inside them while the insect is still alive
When the worm is ready to reproduce, the infected host becomes unusually attracted to light, which may draw it toward the shiny surface of water

title: From 18th-century false ballots to the second JFK and double Dan Sullivans, a brief history of spoiler candidates and the unsuccessful legal challenges to them
