body: This story appeared in  Today, Explained,  a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
Hi readers, happy Friday! We have a big weekend coming up: Halloween, the New York Marathon — and the end of daylight saving time
At 2 am on Sunday, our clocks will fall back one hour, returning us to standard time for the next four and a half months or so

Depending on who you ask, it’s either the welcome return of before-work sunshine, or the start of a dreary slog through 4:30 pm sunsets. (The good news, though, is that however you feel about falling back, it’s  not nearly as hard on the body as springing forward will be in March, when we return to daylight saving time.) It’s also a topic that draws strong opinions, including in the pages of Vox (which has both pointed out the awfulness of daylight saving time and argued that it should go on forever ).  President Donald Trump, of all people, is a strong proponent of the latter view: Several times this month, he’s harangued the US Senate to pass a bill making daylight saving time — that is, the time we’re in from March to early November, with later sunrises and later sunsets — permanent year-round, even posting the personal cellphone number of permanent DST opponent Sen
Tom Cotton (R-AR).  Despite his lobbying, the Senate hasn’t taken action
But should it? Is there a better solution, or are we best off the way things are, despite the burrs? We get into that and more below

Time for the daylight saving time debate View Link As we mentioned above, a bill to establish permanent daylight saving time — the Sunshine Protection Act — is currently on hold in the Senate after passing the House by an overwhelming margin this summer

Nineteen US states have also passed laws that would do the same thing, though they won’t be able to take effect until or unless Congress acts, too. (Two US states, Arizona and Hawaii, are currently on permanent standard time, which is allowed.) Advocates say that more daylight in the evening gives Americans more time to pursue leisure activities after work (the golf industry is a big fan ), plus it may even have some positive effect on crime rates and the economy.  But the utopian ideal of no more darkness before 5 pm may not be all that it’s cracked up to be
Critics of the permanent time change point out that the US has tried permanent DST before, and it was not well received

As the Washingtonian reported in 2022, “While 79 percent of Americans approved of the change in December 1973, approval had  dropped to 42 percent three months later.”  That’s because there’s still only so much sunlight to go around, and permanent DST makes for very dark winter mornings — think sunrises after 9 am along the western edges of time zones

When it took effect in the ’70s, it quickly  proved dangerous for children heading to school in the dark.  As Vox reported in 2016, courtesy of the cartographer Andy Woodruff, the change would leave most people with a  markedly worse sunrise situation in exchange for an after-work boost

If we still want to escape the biannual time change, though, the opposite solution might be preferable: Permanent standard time leaves more people with a reasonable sunrise time, and has  less of an impact on what people described as a reasonable sunset time (really — check out the maps in the story here )

It’s also considered the healthiest option by the  American Academy of Sleep Medicine , which notes that permanent standard time better aligns with our circadian rhythms.  The most likely option, though, is that we keep muddling along like this: Darker evenings are a hard political sell, and Congress abandoned its last permanent DST experiment after less than a year
At least we mostly won’t have to reset our clocks manually on Sunday morning
One link for later ➨ How to do Halloween in a hurry

If you’re short on time and/or money and still in need of a Halloween costume, my colleague Allie Volpe has some advice on ways to tap your creativity (and closet) to pull something off at the last minute

Before you go… Did you know… that some right-wingers, including Vice President JD Vance, are trying to rehabilitate the reputation of President Richard Nixon , who resigned in disgrace after the Watergate scandal and his attempts at a cover-up came to light?  Today’s trivia: Who is the reclusive neighbor to the Finch family in the classic novel To Kill a Mockingbird ? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in Monday’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday, we asked about the name of the vast Andean empire that ruled from its capital in Cusco
That would be the Inca Empire, which covered much of western South America in the 15th and 16th centuries.

title: Forget tainted candy: The scariest thing on Halloween is parked in your driveway
excerpt: As is the custom, millions of children in the United States will be out in the streets this Halloween to trick-or-treat , decked out in costumes
body: As is the custom, millions of children in the United States will be out in the streets this Halloween to trick-or-treat , decked out in costumes
Also as is custom, adults will fret about the mostly mythical dangers children may face
Once upon a time it was razor blades in apples; this year, it’s rainbow fentanyl in candy

But while fears of children receiving narcotic-spiked treats are unfounded , there is a very real danger that America’s children face on this most hallowed of evenings: cars .  That’s because pedestrians under the age of 18 are three times more likely to be struck and killed by a car on Halloween than any other day of the year
A 2026 analysis of federal crash records found that 45 children were killed while walking on Halloween between 2010 and 2024, more than any other day

That risk grows to 10 times more likely for children aged 4 to 8 years old, according to a study from 2019 in JAMA Pediatrics .  National Highway Traffic Safety Administration " data-portal-copyright=" National Highway Traffic Safety Administration " /> “You’re going to have increased numbers of children, including younger children who are out on the streets,” said Lois Lee , a professor of pediatrics and emergency medicine at Harvard Medical School. “At the same time, you have adults who are driving, and especially this year on a Monday, people will be driving home from work

If children are in costume, they may be wearing darker clothing … which makes them harder to detect.” The JAMA Pediatrics study from 2019 corroborates this, noting that Halloween “may heighten pedestrian traffic risk, because celebrations occur at dusk, masks restrict peripheral vision, costumes limit visibility, street-crossing safety is neglected, and some partygoers are impaired by alcohol.” It’s the kind of lethal combination that can turn a fun occasion into a deadly nightmare
Adult victims included, the risk of death to all pedestrians was 43 percent higher on Halloween compared to a regular evening
But what happens on Halloween isn’t an isolated incident
After gun injuries , motor vehicle injuries are the second leading cause of death among children in the US overall

And with pedestrian fatalities (both adult and child) at a 40-year high in the US, it’s worth asking why children roaming the streets is so inherently deadly, and what can be done about it. “Sometimes when you talk about this issue, you get pushback from people and people say, ‘Well, of course, you have more children on the streets, of course, more children are going to die,’” Doug Gordon , a writer and podcast host who advocates for safer streets and cities, told me. “But that accepts a baseline level of danger that I think we as a society have in fact accepted on the other 364 days of the year.” There are broader reasons for why streets have gotten even more dangerous for pedestrians recently
One is that drivers are distracted — not just by their phones, but increasingly by the infotainment systems that come as a part of newer cars

A more pressing issue is the increasing size of cars in the US; SUVs make up half of all car sales in the US, and are much more likely to kill pedestrians in crashes than smaller vehicles. “Mass times [acceleration] is force,” Gordon summed up. “When you increase the mass of something, you’re going to increase the force at which it interacts with a small vulnerable child.”  But the biggest reason may be that American streets and cities are designed for cars , and not people

As Charles Marohn — founder and president of Strong Towns and an expert on urban planning and civil engineering — has argued, engineers who design streets prioritize getting cars as quickly from point A to point B over everything else
One recent example : A traffic safety committee in Utah could not find any way to make the five-lane road crossing to a school safer for students aside from just removing the crosswalk altogether
But there is a lot that can be done to make streets safer, for future Halloweens and every other day of the year

In the short term, cities and towns can build on open streets programs implemented after the Covid-19 pandemic began, which involve closing certain streets to car traffic to allow for more public space
Notably, New York City announced a “Trick or Streets” plan that would see 100 car-free zones in effect from 4 to 8 pm on Halloween this year
And the Big Apple isn’t alone, as Henry Grabar reported for Slate : less dense and more car-dependent cities like St
Petersburg, Florida and Seattle will also either close off the city center for Halloween or actually allow residents to apply for permits that can close off their neighborhoods to car traffic

In the long run, Gordon believes that places around the US should be able to pass what is known as the popsicle test , where a kid should be able to safely walk to a store, buy a popsicle, and return home before it melts

In essence, every city should be designed to be friendly and traversable to the most vulnerable in our communities. “If you start thinking along those lines, then I think you start thinking along the lines of what infrastructure is needed to make that possible, where I would feel comfortable letting my kid do that,” Gordon said. “Halloween is like a giant version of the popsicle test because it’s not just your kid, it’s every kid in the neighborhood.” Designing safer streets for children goes beyond safety — it would make for a better Halloween. “Having sidewalks and good lighting is a good preventive measure, not just for injury prevention, but also just general health,” Lee told me, “because that encourages everybody in the neighborhood to walk, exercise, and get outside, which is better for everybody’s health as well.” And if their safety isn’t enough motivation, designing dense, walkable cities could even lead to bigger candy hauls for kids.  “When you build a city that’s safer, so that kids can walk around by themselves and not be worried about getting hit by a car, or the parents being worried about them being hit by a car, it’s just better,” Gordon said. “It’s awesome
And on Halloween, they get a lot of candy.” Correction, October 31, 4 pm ET: A previous version of this story had an inaccurate definition of the equation for force
Update, October 30, 2026, 10 am ET: This story has been updated to include new federal crash data.

title: The right is rehabbing…Richard Nixon?
excerpt: Former President Richard Nixon puts his hand to his head during an interview with journalist David Frost in April 1977. | John Bryson/Getty Images President Don
body: Former President Richard Nixon puts his hand to his head during an interview with journalist David Frost in April 1977. | John Bryson/Getty Images President Donald Trump is approaching the halfway point of his second term, raising the question of what — and who — comes next

And, more existentially: Can the MAGA movement survive without him? To answer that question, some younger conservatives on the “ New Right ” are looking to a past US president for inspiration: Richard Milhous Nixon.  In June, Vice President JD Vance spoke at the Richard Nixon Presidential Library and Museum in California, downplaying the scandal that ended Nixon’s presidency
If Watergate happened today, Vance said, it would be “like a 12-hour news story

Like, the idea that it would have taken down a presidency is crazy.” Watergate, of course, is the most famous scandal in presidential history and the reason so many of our contemporary imbroglios get tagged with the -gate suffix
It began with a 1972 break-in at the Democratic National Committee’s headquarters in Washington’s Watergate complex by operatives linked to Nixon’s reelection campaign

Investigations — and a huge volume of Oval Office tapes recorded by Nixon — exposed Nixon’s involvement in the cover-up, and he resigned in 1974 facing the prospect of impeachment and removal from office

Nevertheless, some conservatives are now embracing a rehabilitation of Nixon’s image dubbed “ Nixonmaxxing .” They portray him as a president brought down by the “deep state” — an entrenched network of unelected government officials that they believe also tried to undermine Trump during his first term (and is still trying today )

Today, Explained co-host Noel King spoke with political historian Michael Koncewicz , the associate director of New York University’s Institute for Public Knowledge, about what actually brought Nixon down, why Watergate was, in fact, a big deal, and why some conservatives are undeterred and looking to the 37th president for inspiration today
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity

There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify .  Because we live in a fallen world, we are here today to talk about something they’re calling Nixonmaxxing
Why are young conservatives interested in former President Richard Milhous Nixon?  Nixon’s ultimately known for Watergate , and Watergate for decades was the ultimate scandal in American politics

And younger conservatives are starting to revisit this history and they’ve started to compare the Watergate scandal to numerous attempts to bring down the Trump presidency.  Nixon is a martyr for the cause
Nixon is the guy who was successfully brought down by the liberal establishment

And so if younger conservatives can rescue Nixon from liberal historians and liberal journalists, they think that they can protect the current president for decades to come.  In the last decade or so, more and more media figures — and this has seeped down into conservative activists — have questioned a story that most Americans accept, which is that Watergate was a moment where the system worked
It’s a moment where Congress, the media, and the American public helped bring down a corrupt president.  Conservative activists want you to believe that that’s not true
And the main reason is that if they can make you believe that that’s a lie, then they can make you question any future scandal that could affect any one of their guys
What was the Watergate scandal? What did Richard Nixon actually do? Watergate can best be understood as a story that begins, at least, in the summer of 1971

After the release of the Pentagon Papers , which was a secret history of the Vietnam War compiled by figures in the Johnson administration, Richard Nixon is enraged.  In the summer of 1971, the reason that this matters and why it’s linked to Watergate is that in the wake of the Pentagon Papers coming out, Nixon authorizes the creation of the “Plumbers” unit: a group of shady guys with CIA and FBI on their resume, people who have experience doing black bag jobs. “It remains to be seen how influential Nixonmaxxing is as a political phenomenon

Richard Nixon is still seen as one of the worst, most corrupt presidents in American history.” The first operation that they pull off is breaking into Daniel Ellsberg’s psychiatrist’s office — he’s the man who leaked the Pentagon Papers
It’s referred to by Nixon historians as Watergate West
But when they pull this off, they are not caught and it’s dismissed as just a weird moment

No one knows that at the time these are guys being paid by the White House to break into buildings and spy on political opponents.  There’s a lot of other activities that happened between summer of ’71 and June of ’72, but the Watergate burglars, the Plumbers, are caught at the Watergate Hotel
And what is at the Watergate Hotel? It is the offices of the Democratic National Committee

They’re caught in June of ’72, and even then it’s dismissed as a so-called third-rate burglary because this just seems like some overeager campaign staff members who have nothing to do with the Nixon White House
But on the tapes, we know that Richard Nixon, even if he didn’t have any link to the Watergate break-in, knows that he created this team
He knows that his advisers are aware of different parts of their activities over the previous year
That was not uncovered until 1973, which is when most of the American people and most people in Congress started to take this scandal seriously
Watergate ends Nixon’s presidency when it becomes clear to the American people that he has something to hide.  The famous phrase attached to Watergate is that it was not the crime, it’s the coverup
That’s true to an extent, in terms of what was on the tapes that made it very clear that Nixon was obstructing justice
But he was covering up pretty serious crimes
He was covering up a lot of improper uses of presidential power.  And so in the summer and fall of 1973, that is when Richard Nixon’s approval rating started to decline — a 25 percent approval rating
And when people ask why Richard Nixon stepped down, that’s the No. 1 reason
When his approval rating is that low, members of Congress feel the pressure to take on an unprecedented action, which is impeachment
The House was going to impeach Richard Nixon and the Senate was going to convict Richard Nixon.  And so in subsequent years and decades, there’s this understanding that Watergate was a bad thing
Watergate was a serious constitutional crisis and that it was good that Richard Nixon stepped down, that our democracy was strengthened as a result of Watergate
And today’s conservatives are increasingly questioning that narrative

Richard Nixon wouldn’t be in the position he is in currently if he hadn’t done some things that a certain type of conservative today thinks is noble or laudable or important.  What was he doing at the time that makes a guy like Chris Rufo or the vice president say, “Hey, you know what? We need to reconsider Nixon”? Figures like Christopher Rufo are drawn to Richard Nixon because the historical record shows that behind the scenes, he was a fierce culture warrior.  Other presidents in the post-World War II era were certainly guilty of improper uses of presidential power
Nixon’s key difference was he wanted to bring that into the White House and micromanage the hell out of it
And Christopher Rufo loves that about Richard Nixon

He believes that presidents should use their powers to go after groups that he thinks are hurting the country.  We now know that Nixon was a far more aggressive culture warrior behind the scenes.  He was someone who wanted to create a new establishment, one that would weaken liberals in the media

title: Why healthcare has become such a big problem for Republicans
excerpt: A Get Out the Vote rally hosted by the Republican Party of Kentucky took place on October 24, 2026. | Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images Less than
body: A Get Out the Vote rally hosted by the Republican Party of Kentucky took place on October 24, 2026. | Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images Less than a week out from the 2026 midterms, Republicans across the country are feeling the heat from their party’s vote last year to shrink Medicaid by roughly $1 trillion over the next decade
The cuts, driven largely by new work requirements and eligibility checks, are expected to leave more than 7 million Americans without insurance by 2034
They’ll also hit hospitals, clinics, and nursing homes that everyone uses, whether or not they’re on Medicaid
These cuts weren’t supposed to be noticeable to voters just yet
Republicans designed them to take effect in 2027, after the midterms
But some of the damage is already showing up

Paired with a reduction in tax credits to help buy insurance through the Affordable Care Act, and rising employee premiums , the cuts are colliding with a broader voter revolt against the high cost of living — and have turned healthcare into a top midterm issue
A slew of recent polling shows healthcare costs sitting at the top of voters’ economic worries as the campaign season winds down

A KFF poll from earlier this month found healthcare outranked food, housing, and utilities as a top concern, with nearly half of voters saying it was “extremely important” for candidates to be talking about

And in late September, an Associated Press and KFF survey of rural voters found that twice as many said the Trump administration’s healthcare policies had hurt the health of people in their community as said they’d helped.  Key takeaways Healthcare costs top the list of voters’ economic concerns The GOP’s new $50 billion rural fund doesn’t offset $137 billion in rural Medicaid cuts, and the savings come mostly from people losing coverage
Work requirements hit nationwide in 2027, so the first wave of coverage losses lands as the 2028 campaign begins

Republicans have tried to rebrand the One Big Beautiful Bill Act as the “Working Families Tax Cuts,” but Politico found voters largely unmoved by the new name, and Fox News recently gave Democrats a 22-point lead on who voters trust to handle healthcare
Democrats, for their part, have put healthcare costs at the center of their closing argument

It’s the issue they’ve spent more on than any other, according to the Cook Political Report’s Battleground Issue Tracker , with more than $215 million across the  most competitive House and Senate races this year

Democrats trying to flip red seats are running ads on reversing the Medicaid cuts and on having relied on Medicaid once themselves , while outside liberal groups are spending millions of dollars in ad s tying Republicans to the cuts, and leading an 8,000-mile bus tour through 36 cities.  They’ll have even more to work with next year

The new Medicaid work requirements and the six-month eligibility checks that Republicans delayed past the midterms will all take effect in 2027, which means the first wave of people losing health insurance coverage will hit right as the 2028 campaign begins

Republicans’ defenses aren’t holding up Reducing Medicaid spending became a critical part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in order to help offset the multitrillion-dollar cost of extending President Donald Trump’s first-term tax cuts, adding some new ones, and funding ICE
Mindful of the potential for political backlash, Republicans took steps to ward off attacks
The main defense Republicans have relied on is to point to a $50 billion rural health fund that was also included in the bill
The GOP is touting it as “the single largest investment” in rural healthcare in over 20 years

But fact-checkers and health analysts have been clear that this temporary infusion of funds, spread out over five years, doesn’t offset the $137 billion in permanent cuts projected to hit rural areas over the same decade.  Maine Republican Sen

Susan Collins, who voted to let the One Big Beautiful Bill Act reach the Senate floor but against final passage, leaned on this rural healthcare fund in a debate earlier this month. “If I had not allowed the bill to go to the floor, I would never have been able to author the $50 billion fund to help rural healthcare,” she said

Troy Jackson, her Democratic challenger, emphasized that the fund comes nowhere close to covering what Mainers stand to lose. “Senator Collins is like an arsonist who helped set the fire, and then she wants credit for bringing a cup of water to put it out,” he said
Voters don’t need a fact-check to notice when a hospital shuts down or reduces service
In some cases, medical institutions aren’t waiting for the cuts to arrive, and are making decisions based on the federal funding they expect to lose

In Iowa, for example, MercyOne Clinton Medical Center ended labor and delivery services earlier this year, citing decreased Medicaid funding as part of the reason. “The public’s not stupid, and we’re all already absorbing a lot of additional costs that we shouldn’t have to because of Republican decision-making in Washington, DC,” Michigan Gov
The second is to deny there is reduced spending at all. “It’s not an actual cut,” as GOP Rep

David Valadao of California said in a debate several weeks ago — the savings, Republicans argue, come from cracking down on waste, fraud, and abuse .  This distinction is an important one in certain campaigns
Medicaid covers over 60 percent of Valadao’s California district, and he voted for the bill

Valadao also led a letter , signed by 12 other Republicans from battleground districts, declaring that “we cannot and will not support a final reconciliation bill that includes any reduction in Medicaid coverage for vulnerable populations.” Every one of them ultimately voted for it.  Loss of coverage is already happening in Nebraska, the only state to start enforcing its new Medicaid work requirements ahead of the deadline
The “no actual cuts” claim rests on a technicality that the law doesn’t reduce benefits for anyone who stays enrolled
But the roughly $1 trillion in savings the Congressional Budget Office scored comes almost entirely from people losing coverage
When Arkansas tried the same 80-hour-a-month work requirement in 2018, more than 18,000 people lost their health insurance within months
This happened mostly because people didn’t know about the changes or couldn’t handle the new paperwork
Loss of coverage is already happening in Nebraska, the only state to start enforcing its new Medicaid work requirements ahead of the deadline
Millions more across the country are getting notices in the mail that they could lose their insurance next year
The problems driving voter anger are about to get worse Nebraska offers the clearest preview of what’s coming
The state began enforcing its Medicaid work requirements in July, well ahead of the federal deadline, and more than 1,000 residents have already lost coverage, according to the Washington Sun

Pete Ricketts, who voted for the bill, is tied with Dan Osborn , an independent, in a state that Trump carried easily. “One out of two Republicans either are, have been or have a family member that is or has been on Medicaid,” Bob Ward, a pollster with the GOP firm Fabrizio Ward, told the Washington Sun. “It’s not like a theoretical thing.” The rest of the country will experience these new administrative burdens beginning in January

Adults covered under the Medicaid expansion will have to prove every six months that they’re working, volunteering, or attending classes at least 80 hours per month, or demonstrate that they qualify for an exception

title: Democrats can do something about energy prices — without winning the midterms
excerpt: A great deal is at stake in next week’s midterm elections
body: A great deal is at stake in next week’s midterm elections
The partisan makeup of the new Congress will shape future spending bills, congressional investigations, and judicial nominations, among other things
And yet, the most consequential bill of the next 12 months — and the one that speaks most directly to voters’ concerns about the cost-of-living — might well pass before the new Congress is seated
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) could dramatically reshape America’s energy system

And the bill’s supporters plan to pass it during the House and Senate’s lame-duck session — the months between next week’s elections and the new Congress’s arrival.  The bill is long and complex, revising the rules governing everything from how ocean-powered turbines are licensed to what some geothermal plants must pay in royalties .  That said, the legislation’s fundamental aim is simple: to make building all forms of energy infrastructure easier.  The BAAJA has united fossil fuel companies and green energy firms in its favor — while cleaving the climate movement in two
Key takeaways The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act would make it easier to build new power plants and transmission lines
The bill benefits fossil fuel companies, but it would likely do even more to accelerate the growth of clean energy
Environmentalists are divided over the bill, with critics warning that it would weaken important environmental protections
The bill has one potentially serious flaw that Congress should fix
But with that change, it would be a win for the climate and consumers alike

Some climate hawks contend that the legislation pares back vital environmental regulations , while clearing the way for new gas pipelines and power plants that will drive up America’s emissions. “This is not the permitting deal that we were promised,” Jeremy Symons, president of the Center for Energy and Environmental Analysis, told me, citing its “historic environmental protection rollbacks.” Others insist that the bill is a net-win for decarbonization

In their account, permitting reforms will do more to facilitate a buildout of green energy than to lock in America’s dependence on fossil fuels.  “Fossil is the incumbent technology and fuel mix,” Jane Flegal, a senior fellow at the center-left Searchlight Institute, said. “A system that makes it easier for everyone to build should advantage the nonincumbent.” I think Flegal’s side has this right
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act will likely help renewables erode fossil fuels’ share of the electricity market
By itself, the legislation will not ensure a timely transition to a green electricity system
But it will get us a little further down that road, while also making energy more affordable for US consumers — which might well be the midterm electorate’s top priority
This said, the current draft of the bill does contain one potentially major — and seemingly, accidental — flaw
Assuming Congress fixes that issue, climate hawks should join hands with Big Oil and push for the BAAJA’s imminent passage

A carbon-free electric grid requires a lot of infrastructure  The climate case for permitting reform begins with a simple observation: If you want to decarbonize America’s energy grid, you need to build a metric fudge-ton of new infrastructure
Today, low-carbon energy sources provide about 43 percent of our nation’s electricity

Thus, even if America embraced “degrowth” — and froze its electricity consumption at current levels — zeroing out the power sector’s carbon emissions would require constructing a gargantuan number of new wind, solar, battery storage, and geothermal (and/or nuclear) projects.  But of course, America is not actually going to freeze its use of electricity
And mainstream climate hawks don’t even want it to
After all, if every SUV owner replaces their gas guzzler with an EV, then demand for electricity will rise
And decarbonizing home heat or heavy industry will have the same effect
Indeed, to an extent, this basic process is already playing out. “We’re seeing quite rapid demand growth,” Flegal said. “And that is not only — or even primarily — because of data centers

It’s because of broader structural trends toward electrifying our economy and onshoring manufacturing.” Taking demand growth into account, a study from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) estimated that getting to a carbon-free electric grid by 2035 would require generating roughly 2,000 gigawatts of wind and solar energy; today, we generate roughly 396 gigawatts.  The challenge appears even more formidable when measured in land

According to Princeton’s 2021 Net Zero America estimate, in a “high electrification” scenario, the US will need wind and solar developments that collectively span nearly 600,000 square kilometers of land — roughly the size of California and Washington state combined
And even this may undersell the scale of the task

Achieving net zero does not only require constructing immense quantities of wind turbines and solar panels — complemented by battery storage and firm power sources like nuclear or geothermal — but also a vast network of new transmission lines
America’s transmission infrastructure is already inadequate to our current electricity needs
But a carbon-free grid would demand far more high-voltage lines than today’s
This is because fossil fuel plants are more geographically flexible than renewable ones
Per unit of power generated, gas plants require a small fraction of the land that wind and solar do
And in regions with mature pipeline networks, gas plants can be located in a wide range of places
For these reasons, it’s not that difficult to site carbon power facilities near major population centers or existing transmission lines
By contrast, wind and solar farms need to be located in areas with both favorable weather conditions and a great deal of affordable land
Such sites are often far from the urban areas where electricity is most needed
Therefore, to replace fossil fuels with renewable energy, America will need a lot more transmission lines

According to NREL, to achieve a 100 percent clean electric grid by 2035 would require building between 1,400 and 10,000 miles of high-capacity transmission lines annually; in 2024, America built just 888 miles

Given all this, a permitting system that’s biased toward stasis is one that’s biased toward fossil fuels: The harder it is to build new power plants and transmission lines, the longer our electric grids will need to rely on carbon energy
This world was built for fossil fuels Alas, the current permitting regime does, in fact, make building power infrastructure really hard

title: The Download: AI agent tracking and climate feedback loops
excerpt: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
Opinion: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time —Madhulika Srikumar and Claire Leibowicz from the Partnership on AI, a nonprofit advancing best practices in AI governance
AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, from hacking websites to accessing private government files

In many cases, they’ve eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.  As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent potentially devastating consequences
And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability . ​​In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it
Because right now, we’re effectively flying blind when deploying these tools.  Here’s what needs to change
Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot Climate change itself increasingly fuels climate change
Rising greenhouse gas concentrations are driving up global temperatures, creating dangerous feedback loops that aren’t fully represented in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals
Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming
Now, a growing number of observations and studies are indicating how powerful these cascading effects could be
By extension, they’re also showing how much faster the planet may warm this century
Read more about the dangerous feedback loops accelerating global warming . —James Temple This article is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter
Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday

Are we there yet? Solid-state batteries  Lithium-ion batteries power everything from personal electronics to grid-scale energy storage, but their liquid electrolytes have drawbacks, not least a troubling tendency to catch fire
Enter the solid-state battery, which swaps liquid for a solid ceramic or polymer
The technology promises faster charging, longer life, greater energy density and improved safety, and a new generation of companies aims to bring it to market
If their bets pan out, the tech could ease the shift away from fossil fuels
Find out how close solid-state batteries are to delivering on their promise . —Alexander C
Kaufman This story is part of “Are we there yet?” , our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter
We’re exploring each one in The Download, so stay tuned, and subscribe to read the rest of the stories in our new Impossible issue

The must-reads I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology. 1 Hackers exposed 41,000 Homeland Security workers Including undercover ICE agents. ( CNN ) + Steve Jobs and Tim Cook had both dismissed the idea. ( NYT $) + Executives say touchscreen advances mean it’s now worthwhile. ( Wired $) 4 Bloomberg and trading firms are paying to get Trump’s posts faster They’ve signed up for Truth Social’s pay-for-access plan. ( Gizmodo ) Quote of the day “ They have our information, so it’s only fair that we have theirs.”  —A hacking group explains why it leaked personal information from the US Department of Homeland Security, NPR reports
One more thing How the Pentagon is adapting to China’s technological rise It’s been just over a year since Kathleen Hicks stepped down as US deputy secretary of defense

As the highest-ranking woman in Pentagon history, Hicks shaped US military posture through an era defined by renewed competition between powerful countries and a scramble to modernize defense technology

title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
excerpt: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test
body: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test
They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded
Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website
It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI
In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track

And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.  AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts
That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time

But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility.  Imagine a bank hiring a thousand new employees who can access customer accounts and sensitive information, but the employees’ ID badges change every day, it’s not clear whether a manager ever reviewed or authorized their work, and nobody logs the changes employees make to approval processes
That lack of visibility is where we are with agents today

As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine , we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences.  And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability : the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems
In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it
And as our recent research shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely
Agents present new kinds of problems that generative AI alone does not

They inherit the unpredictability of the LLMs they are built on, but where a generative AI system produces a single output for a human to act on, an agent performs longer tasks—it plans, picks tools, spawns sub-agents, and takes actions
So an agent’s course can take shape in a multitude of different ways, and no tests before launch can fully anticipate the risks
This makes observing the agents while they work even more challenging, and even more important
With colleagues from academia, civil society, and industry, we studied the four most widely used agent frameworks to see what signals they actually emit
We found major gaps that made it hard to achieve key safety goals, like noticing policy violations, unauthorized actions, and even human oversight failures
Key observability requirements were missing—like Agent IDs that persist over time, and records about which humans approved agent tasks
This made it hard to tell which agents did what or assess whether they were taking unauthorized actions.  The good news is that these gaps, once identified, can be closed
Doing so starts with capturing two types of records: those that reveal what happened in an agent’s run and how the agent made its decisions

The “what happened” records identify the agent (while preserving privacy) and log how humans intervened and whether agent permissions or “memory” shifted, while the “decision” records show an agent’s reasoning and levels of confidence in the actions it’s taken
Take, for example, agents working to process a bank’s mortgage loans
The system examines an application and recommends denying it, and then a human loan officer signs off on the decision
In a later audit, or perhaps even in real time, a bank or regulator needs to be able to reconstruct which agent made the call, which officer approved it, and how long they took

And the bank must also analyze records of how the agent arrived at its refusal decision in order to ensure it did not use off-limits information, like details about the neighborhood the applicant is from
Recording “what happened” and “how the agent decided” require different approaches, but both are feasible

The current lack of “what happened” records is mostly a software plumbing problem that can be addressed through OpenTelemetry, an open observability standard maintained by engineers across the industry and by the agent frameworks adopting it
OpenTelemetry has launched a working group drafting shared formats for tracing agents, but they have yet to be finalized
The group should urgently incorporate standards for maintaining persistent agent identity and for recording human interventions and changes to agents’ permission or memory
And it should be done before these systems can scale, all the while attending to the privacy implications of agent ID that links to real people
Preserving “how agents decided” records is more challenging

The issue raises open research questions for model providers and researchers: Does the step-by-step reasoning a model displays, known as chain of thought, reflect how the model actually made a decision? And do we have reliable ways to measure how confident the agent is in that decision? These questions need answers before anyone sets standards for how such observability records are used

No single organization or sector can close the observability gaps on their own, but together, they can support the infrastructure required to prevent dangerous incidents and support safety.  AI developers building agent frameworks, like OpenAI, Anthropic, CrewAI, and LangChain, must integrate telemetry signals recording an agent’s persistent identity, any human interventions, and any changes to an agent’s permissions and memory

Meanwhile, enterprises adopting these agent frameworks have an influential role to play; enterprises in regulated industries, like banks and hospitals, can put pressure on the agent developers to supply these missing observability records where standards do not yet exist
Enterprises must also define policies, permissions, and roles that set out what agents can safely do, since telemetry alone cannot assess whether agents broke specific rules
Finally, regulators and AI standards institutes must specify the observability records required for high-stakes AI deployments while leaving the technical details to industry

We have already seen initial momentum here: NIST’s agent standards initiative in the US is working on agent identity, one of the most salient gaps we found in our research.  No bank would let a thousand unbadged employees loose on customer accounts and hope to piece together what happened when something goes wrong
Making their behavior observable is the first step toward fixing this
And by building the regulatory and policy ecosystem that makes it possible to act on what we see, we can hold organizations accountable

title: Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
excerpt: A dangerous blind spot in climate models: Current models used to inform major UN climate reports fail to account for powerful feedback loops—where warming itsel
body: A dangerous blind spot in climate models: Current models used to inform major UN climate reports fail to account for powerful feedback loops—where warming itself drives more warming—leaving us underestimating how fast temperatures could rise
The numbers are alarming: Thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, warming wetlands and other feedbck effects could add 0.2°C to 0.4°C of extra warming this century

Scientists are scrambling to catch up: Over 20 international research teams are now running coordinated analyses to better understand these feedback effects, with hopes the UN will incorporate findings into its next major climate assessment in 2029. " data-chronoton-post-id="1147735" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change

Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals

Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be
And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century

A study in Environmental Research Letters in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, hotter lakes and reservoirs , and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century
That would come on top of the 2.6°C of warming above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100

The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to monthslong heat waves and expose hundreds of millions of people to flooding.  None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects

That leaves a huge blind spot in our understanding of how much the world could actually warm in the coming decades—and how rapidly nations will need to slash emissions to stay within critical boundaries

A separate analysis published in One Earth in March , which examined what the feedback problem means for our international climate goals, concluded that the world may be much further off track than is widely believed

It found that just three regional sources of warming-driven emissions—thawing permafrost, increasing fires in boreal forests, and warming tropical wetlands—may shorten by as much as 25% the time before the planet consistently breaches the 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming thresholds
Our climate models and the UN’s reports clearly need to be updated to better represent these effects

Nations must also step up their efforts to reduce emissions to reflect this improving understanding of the dangers we face, says Sam Abernethy, the lead author of the paper and a climate scientist at Spark Climate Solutions, a San Francisco–based nonprofit research group.  At least some of this is starting to happen

Spark kick-started an initiative, called the Warming-Induced Greenhouse Gas Emissions Model Intercomparison Project , through which more than 20 international teams are running the same set of analyses on different models to develop greater understanding of feedback effects’ potential power
Researchers involved hope that the UN will incorporate those results into its next major climate assessment, due out in 2029
That report will update estimates of the remaining emissions that can be released before the world crosses key temperature thresholds
But what is already clear is that the planet is rapidly warming and that nations haven’t done nearly enough to cut fossil-fuel pollution

And even if we did manage to halt it, warming-driven emissions could continue.  So a number of the research groups involved in the recent studies have started to explore what nations could do to get feedback emissions under control

Scientists at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Massachusetts are, for example, investigating the possibility of preventing fires or rapidly detecting them and putting them out when they threaten to burn the vegetation and soil that help insulate particularly carbon-rich wedges of permafrost (a subject I explored at length in a recent feature story )

In addition, the Environmental Defense Fund’s Climate Innovation Initiative has backed lab research on the potential of adding sulfate, iron, or other compounds to wetlands to counteract fast-rising methane emissions.  Several startups are also exploring possibilities

They’re looking into suppressing the lightning strikes that are igniting more and more fires in high latitudes, placing synthetic mats above permafrost to prevent it from melting, and deploying autonomous drones to quickly suppress potentially high-emissions fires before they burn out of control
Investigating all these ideas is worthwhile

But researchers are only in the earliest stages of figuring out how big a dent in emissions any such efforts could achieve across sprawling global ecosystems undergoing massive transformations.  The surest path to reducing the effect of warming-driven warming remains the one we’ve known all along: breaking society’s addiction to fossil fuels.  This article is from The Spark,  MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter
To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday,   sign up here .

title: The case for a little election optimism
excerpt: President Donald Trump arrives to speak at a midterm campaign rally in Corpus Christi, Texas on October 27, 2026. | Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images This sto
body: President Donald Trump arrives to speak at a midterm campaign rally in Corpus Christi, Texas on October 27, 2026. | Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here

No sooner had early voting started this year than analysts noticed a curious trend: Democratic voters were choosing to vote a lot like…Republicans.  Since the Covid-19 pandemic, Democrats who cast their ballots early have most commonly done so by mail
But this year, they’re voting in person , and in huge numbers — even narrowing Republicans’ traditional early voting lead in states like Florida and Texas

The abrupt shift may have something to do with President Donald Trump’s attempts to undermine the mail voting process , and it almost definitely reflects the anxiety and vigilance that many Americans feel about the midterms this year

In less than a week, they’ll decide which party controls Congress, along with a slew of state and local offices.  The stakes are arguably unusually high: Voters will choose whether to check the power of a president who has bulldozed over historical norms and limits

So as we count down to that momentous and potentially messy day, I’ve been partnering with my colleague Astead Herndon and Vox’s The Midterms, Actually team for a series of weekly editions on the biggest issues shaping the midterms.  Previously, we dug into the ways both parties are changing , the bipartisan backlash to AI and data centers , the politics of high costs, and the changing mood toward Israel
This week, for our final installment, we’re tackling something a little more fundamental: the integrity and security of the voting process itself
It’s a worrying subject, but by no means a hopeless one
Go a little deeper Let me begin with a metaphor that may or may not reassure you: Imagine there’s a serial killer outside your house, and they’re trying to get in and kill you
That’s pretty terrifying, under any circumstance
But also: Your house is an absolute vault

And the police are actually on its way now. “I don’t want to understate the threat” of election interference, Benjy Sarlin, Vox’s editorial director of politics said when he relayed this metaphor  on the America, Actually podcast last month
But if Trump is the serial killer trying America’s doors and windows…then understand this house is pretty well-defended.  Take mail voting, the issue that has so (literally) moved Democrats this year

You’ll recall that Trump tried to sabotage the practice by implementing new, last-minute rules that would have effectively canceled mail-in voting in some places.  But the Constitution clearly assigns the power to regulate and administer elections to the states and Congress, and courts blocked the administration’s rules
In mid-September, the Supreme Court declined to let them take effect for this election
So there’s one lock made good.  The Trump administration has also demanded unprecedented access to states’ voter rolls, suing 30 states and Washington, DC, to obtain them
Of those cases, courts have dismissed 27 of them (though many dismissals are being appealed)
Earlier this month, the DOJ went further and demanded that California officials  set aside the ballots of some 20,000 registered voters that it alleged were likely noncitizens
In the predictable legal battle that followed, courts sided with the state

A federal judge excoriated the administration in an opinion on Wednesday , ruling that the ballot segregation order “would wreak havoc and disrupt the election.” The Trump administration has already appealed the ruling.  Other forms of meddling are possible

Asked in August about declaring a national emergency to impose new voting requirements, Trump replied — unnervingly — that “stranger things have happened.” And the president and his allies have floated drastic measures like deploying federal agents to polling sites or seizing “suspect” ballots, a threat tangible enough that it’s reportedly unsettled a number of FBI agents.  Just last week, the Trump administration attempted to preemptively contest the results in Alaska’s Senate race, claiming that the presence of two Dan Sullivans on the ballot — the incumbent Republican and an independent newcomer — risked confusing voters
The New York Times has since reported that Democrats enticed Dan Sullivan 2.0 to run for exactly that reason
In some corners, the ensuing scandal has raised concerns that Republicans could refuse to seat Democrat Mary Peltola if she wins.  But even that possibility is fairly remote
While there are mechanisms for both state officials and US lawmakers to challenge election results, those procedures are pretty regimented

And any attempts to disrupt voting, vote-counting, or the certification of results would likely face both a flood of lawsuits (which voting groups have already prepped ) and a public outcry that could ultimately and lastingly hurt Republicans
Trump might not care overmuch about democratic norms or the rule of law, but he does likely care about the risks of a longer-term political backlash

To this day, Benjy said, a lot of Republicans still blame Trump for losing them Georgia’s Senate seats: His election denialism after 2020 helped drive huge numbers of Black Georgians to the polls, where they voted in two Democrats.  The number of Democrats voting early and in-person suggests the possibility that a similar dynamic is at play now

In other words, there is real risk — but lots of people are fighting to keep the proverbial bad guys out.  Races to watch: Alaska Senate race, where Trump is ready to contest a Democratic win ; Wisconsin governor’s race, where  Republican Tom Tiffany has promoted Trump’s lies about the 2020 election;  Nevada’s secretary of state race, which could similarly put an outspoken election denier in charge of the state’s voting system
More from Vox:  How election officials are thinking about Trump’s threat to the midterms The one thing everyone can do to fight for free and fair elections Trump has a plan to steal the midterms
One link for later ➨ Turn on the (early morning) lights
It’s getting darker earlier and earlier these days, and it’s often pitch black when my alarm goes off
That means it’s time for an annual tradition: digging out my bulky, 10,000-lux light box
Bright morning light, from a box or the sun, sets your body’s internal clock and helps regulate your sleep

It can also mitigate seasonal affective disorder, which starts plaguing many sufferers around Halloween.   Before you go… Did you know… that there’s an extremely rare and spooky form of lightning that can appear indoors? It’s called “ball lightning,” and it’s one of the most mysterious weather phenomena in the world.   Today’s trivia: What’s the name of the vast Andean empire that ruled from its capital in Cusco? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you where you might find an arroyo
These seasonally dry streambeds cut through deserts, where they can serve as a “highway” for wild animals.

title: Creating AI value with enterprise context
excerpt: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assis
body: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools
Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond
But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a proper understanding of the business
Many organizations find themselves in this situation—and it could be one of key reasons they struggle to extract returns on their AI investments

DOWNLOAD THE REPORT An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments

The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all
Companies are mostly still piloting AI use cases (according to 38% of respondents) or using it to assist employees’ work with tools like co-pilots or chat assistants (35%)

Just 12% of enterprises have AI agents in production and 3% say they are using AI to do most of the work in key processes. “There’s a big gap between what the models are capable of and how the models are actually being useful inside organizations,” says Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan. “For every real-life intent and purpose, artificial general intelligence is already here
It’s just not really useful in most companies today.” The missing layer, Sankar says, is context, or how well AI understands a business
A context layer is the architectural infrastructure that sits between an organization’s business systems (for example, systems of record and data, and its AI platforms)

It translates enterprise intelligence into governed, machine-usable context for AI agents or models and helps knowledge compound. “Without a context layer for AI, it’s almost like you’re hiring the smartest intern in the world, blindfolding them, and throwing them into your organization,” Sankar says

It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

body: Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected to travel ban and asset freeze Senior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of a mass atrocity that saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days
